stem: Which choice describes what the whole passage does, not just one sentence of it?
stimulus: The theremin, invented by the Russian physicist Léon Theremin around 1920, is one of the few instruments played without being touched. The performer moves one hand near an upright antenna to change the pitch and the other hand near a looped antenna to change the volume. Its eerie, wavering tone made it a favorite of film composers in the 1950s, who used it to signal the arrival of aliens and other strange visitors.
choices: To describe an unusual instrument, including how it is played and used
To explain how a theremin player controls the volume of each note
To argue that the theremin deserves more respect from trained musicians
To compare the theremin with instruments that are played by touch
explanation: Ask what every sentence has in common. The first says what the theremin is, the second says how it is played, and the third says how it was used. Together they describe one instrument, and only choice A covers all three sentences. Finding what the whole text does, rather than what one sentence does, is the skill behind 'main purpose' questions that profile a person, work, or thing.

B.why: You picked a detail that is really in the text, since the looped antenna does control volume. But it is half of one sentence. A purpose has to cover the whole passage, and this choice leaves out where the instrument came from and how it was used.

C.why: You chose a verb that is too strong. 'Argue' needs an opinion in the text, and this passage only gives facts. Nothing in it says musicians fail to respect the theremin or should respect it more.

D.why: You accepted a comparison the text never makes. The passage says the theremin is played without touch, but it never discusses any other instruments or sets them side by side with it.

stem: Which choice describes what the whole passage does, not just one sentence of it?
stimulus: The mimic octopus, first recorded off the coast of Indonesia in 1998, survives by pretending to be other animals. When it spreads its striped arms and drifts, it resembles a venomous lionfish. When it hides six arms in the sand and waves the other two, it looks like a banded sea snake. It can also flatten its body and glide along the seafloor like a flatfish.
choices: To explain when and where the mimic octopus was first recorded
To argue that the mimic octopus is the cleverest animal in the ocean
To describe how one octopus imitates several different sea animals
To show that the octopus imitates only animals that are venomous
explanation: Cover any one sentence and ask what the others share. Every sentence after the first gives an example of the octopus copying another animal: a lionfish, a sea snake, a flatfish. Choice C names that shared job. Spotting the thread that runs through a list of examples is the first step in any 'main purpose' question about a profile.

A.why: You took a true detail from the opening clause as the purpose. The date and place appear once and are never mentioned again, while the rest of the passage is about imitation.

B.why: You chose a choice that claims far more than the text does. The passage describes what the octopus does. It never ranks the octopus against other animals or calls it the cleverest.

D.why: You missed the last sentence. A flatfish is not venomous, so the passage itself shows that the octopus copies more than venomous animals.

stem: Which choice describes what the whole passage does, not just one sentence of it?
stimulus: For centuries, physicians regarded the thymus, a small organ behind the breastbone, as having no real purpose. In 1961, however, the immunologist Jacques Miller showed that mice whose thymus was removed shortly after birth developed badly weakened immune systems. Researchers now know that the thymus is where T cells, a type of white blood cell, mature before they travel through the body to fight infection.
choices: To describe how an organ once thought useless was found to matter
To explain the method Miller used in his experiments on young mice
To argue that physicians should study other organs thought useless
To show that physicians today still regard the thymus as useless
explanation: The passage moves from an old belief (the thymus has no purpose) to a 'however' (Miller's finding) to today's understanding (T cells mature there). All three sentences trace how ideas about one organ changed, and choice A covers that whole arc. Reading past the old belief to the correction that follows is the move you need for 'main purpose' questions built on an 'old view, then the correction' pattern.

B.why: You focused on the middle sentence alone. Miller's experiment is one piece of evidence in the story, and the passage gives only one line about it. It is not what the whole text is for.

C.why: You took a recommendation the text never makes. The passage reports a discovery about one organ and says nothing about what physicians should study next or about any other organ.

D.why: You stopped at the first sentence and missed the 'however.' The old belief is the view the passage corrects. The last sentence shows that researchers now know what the thymus does.

stem: Which choice describes what the whole passage does, not just one sentence of it?
stimulus: In the 1950s, the geologist Marie Tharp turned thousands of sonar depth readings into the first detailed maps of the ocean floor. Working with Bruce Heezen, she drew the Atlantic seafloor as a landscape of mountains, plains, and canyons. Her maps revealed a deep valley running along the center of an undersea mountain range, a finding that helped convince scientists that continents slowly move. In 1977, she and Heezen published a map of the entire ocean floor.
choices: To describe a mapmaker's work and what her ocean-floor maps revealed
To explain how sonar measures the depth of water beneath a ship
To identify the year in which Tharp's map of the whole ocean appeared
To argue that Heezen deserves more credit than Tharp for the maps
explanation: Every sentence is about Tharp's maps: how she made them, what they showed, what they revealed, and what she published later. Choice A covers both her work and its findings, so it fits the whole passage. Finding the purpose of a profile of a person is exactly what you need for 'main purpose' questions about artists, scientists, and inventors.

B.why: You picked a topic that the passage mentions but does not explain. Sonar readings were Tharp's raw material, and the text never describes how sonar works.

C.why: You picked a true detail that is too narrow. The 1977 map appears only in the last sentence, so naming its year leaves out the rest of the passage.

D.why: You chose an argument the text never makes. Heezen is named as Tharp's partner, but the passage gives no opinion on who deserves credit. 'Argue' is too strong a verb for a passage that only informs.

stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
stimulus: Tactile maps let people who are blind or have low vision read a place with their fingertips. Instead of using colors, these maps show roads as raised lines, parks as dotted textures, and water as smooth, flat areas. Labels are printed in braille. Some cities now mount tactile maps in train stations so that riders can find platforms and exits on their own.
choices: To explain why parks appear as dotted textures on tactile maps
To describe what tactile maps are and how people use them
To argue that every train station should install a tactile map
To describe how tactile maps use color to show roads and water
explanation: Ask what every sentence has in common. The first sentence says what tactile maps are. The middle sentences say how they show roads, parks, water and labels. The last sentence says where people use them. Each one gives a fact about tactile maps, and none of them gives an opinion, so the neutral verb 'describe' fits. Only this choice covers the whole text. This is the first step on any 'main purpose' question about a profile of a person, work or thing: find what all the sentences share before you look at the choices.

A.why: The dotted textures for parks really are in the text, but they come up in only one part of one sentence. You picked a true detail instead of a purpose that covers the whole passage. The text also never explains why parks are shown that way. It only says that they are.

C.why: You matched the topic but not the tone. The text says only that 'some cities' use tactile maps in stations. It never says that every station should have one. 'Argue' needs a clear opinion in the text, and this passage only gives information.

D.why: This choice reverses the text. The passage says tactile maps work 'instead of using colors' and use raised lines and textures. If you skimmed past 'instead of', you may have expected an ordinary map with colors.
